afar-triangle.name: Afar Depression
afar-triangle.summary: A geological depression in East Africa's Great Rift Valley, bordering Eritrea, Djibouti and Ethiopia, containing Africa's lowest point and sites that have yielded some of the earliest known fossil hominins.

ajuran-sultanate.name: Ajuran Sultanate
ajuran-sultanate.summary: A Muslim empire in the Horn of Africa, founded by Somali sultans, that rose to prominence in the 13th and 14th centuries and became Africa's only known 'hydraulic empire,' resisting Oromo and Portuguese incursions.

zeila.name: Zeila
zeila.summary: A historic port town in what is now Somaliland, capital of the early Adal Kingdom by the 9th century and the Ifat Sultanate in the 13th, later under Ottoman and then British control.

khat.name: Khat
khat.summary: A flowering shrub native to eastern and southern Africa whose leaves are chewed as a mild stimulant causing sociability and euphoria; long cultivated in Ethiopia and widely consumed in Somalia and Yemen.

ethiopian-orthodox-tewahedo-church.name: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church
ethiopian-orthodox-tewahedo-church.summary: The largest Oriental Orthodox church, tracing back to the Christianization of Aksum in 330 CE, with tens of millions of adherents and one of only a few Oriental Orthodox churches in Africa.

kingdom-of-kaffa.name: Kingdom of Kaffa
kingdom-of-kaffa.summary: A kingdom in the Ethiopian highlands from 1390 to 1897, homeland of the coffee plant and origin of its name, conquered and annexed by the Ethiopian Empire under Menelik II.

hormuz-island.name: Hormuz Island
hormuz-island.summary: An Iranian island in the Persian Gulf, occupied by the Portuguese from 1515 until the Safavids conquered it with English help in 1622.

duarte-barbosa.name: Duarte Barbosa
duarte-barbosa.summary: A Portuguese writer and official in Portuguese India (c. 1480–1521) whose account of the region was among the earliest Portuguese travel literature; he died during Magellan's circumnavigation voyage.

gujarat-sultanate.name: Gujarat Sultanate
gujarat-sultanate.summary: A late medieval Indian kingdom based in Gujarat, established in 1394 and known to Portuguese traders as the Kingdom of Cambaya, until its annexation by the Mughal emperor Akbar in 1573.

afgooye.name: Afgooye
afgooye.summary: One of the oldest towns on Somalia's lower Shebelle valley, a trade centre under the Silcis Dynasty and later Ajuran rule, before becoming capital of the Geledi Sultanate in the late 1600s.

kismayo.name: Kismayo
kismayo.summary: A port city in southern Somalia and de facto capital of the autonomous Jubaland region, ruled in the Middle Ages by the Ajuran Empire and later by the Geledi Sultanate and Boqow dynasty.

beilul.name: Beilul
beilul.summary: A small Red Sea port town in Eritrea that served as the historical main port of the Kingdom of Dankali and a link to the outside world.

mokha.name: Mokha
mokha.summary: A Red Sea port city in Yemen that was the principal port for Yemen's capital and, from the 16th to 19th centuries, the world's main marketplace for coffee, giving its name to 'mocha'.

james-bruce.name: James Bruce
james-bruce.summary: A Scottish traveller and writer (1730-1794) who in 1770 became the first European to trace the Nile upstream from Egypt to its source in the Blue Nile in Ethiopia.

afar-region.name: Afar Region
afar-region.summary: A regional state in northeastern Ethiopia, homeland of the Afar people, spanning the low-lying Afar Triangle and Danakil Depression, with the Awash River valley to its south.

adal-sultanate.name: Adal Sultanate
adal-sultanate.summary: Medieval Muslim empire in the Horn of Africa, flourishing roughly 1415–1577, whose long wars with Christian Abyssinia drew in Ottoman and Portuguese forces.

rasulid-dynasty.name: Rasulid dynasty
rasulid-dynasty.summary: Sunni Yemeni dynasty that ruled Yemen from 1229 to 1454.

al-shihr.name: Al-Shihr
al-shihr.summary: A walled coastal town in Hadhramaut, eastern Yemen, with a beach anchorage and markets, whose main export was fish oil.

lalibela.name: Lalibela
lalibela.summary: A town in Ethiopia's Amhara Region famed for rock-cut monolithic churches traditionally dated to the reign of King Gebre Meskel Lalibela (r. c. 1181-1221); one of Ethiopia's holiest pilgrimage sites.

gebre-meskel-lalibela.name: Gebre Meskel Lalibela
gebre-meskel-lalibela.summary: King of Ethiopia's Zagwe dynasty from 1181 to 1221, credited as the patron of the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela and venerated as a saint by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church.

zagwe-dynasty.name: Zagwe dynasty
zagwe-dynasty.summary: A medieval Agaw monarchy ruling parts of Ethiopia and Eritrea from about 1137 to 1270 CE, famed for King Lalibela's rock-hewn churches; its last king, Za-Ilmaknun, was killed in battle.

kingdom-of-aksum.name: Kingdom of Aksum
kingdom-of-aksum.summary: A powerful trading kingdom in the Horn of Africa and South Arabia, founded around the 1st century, ranked among the era's four great powers, and one of the first states to adopt Christianity, in the 4th century.

tigray-region.name: Tigray Region
tigray-region.summary: The northernmost regional state of Ethiopia, homeland of the Tigrayan, Irob and Kunama peoples, with Mekelle as its capital.

vasco-da-gama.name: Vasco da Gama
vasco-da-gama.summary: Portuguese explorer (c. 1460s-1524) whose 1497-1499 voyage opened the first sea route from Europe to India around Africa's Cape of Good Hope.

ibn-battuta.name: Ibn Battuta
ibn-battuta.summary: A Maghrebi Muslim traveller and scholar (1304–1368/69) from Tangier who journeyed about 117,000 km across Africa, Asia and the Iberian Peninsula and dictated an account of his travels, the Rihla.

church-of-saint-george-lalibela.name: Church of Saint George, Lalibela
church-of-saint-george-lalibela.summary: One of eleven rock-hewn monolithic churches in Lalibela, Ethiopia, commissioned by the Zagwe king Gebre Mesqel Lalibela, who is regarded as a saint.

tuff.name: Tuff
tuff.summary: Rock formed when volcanic ash from an eruption hardens into stone. It is fairly soft, so it has been used for building since ancient times, including by the Romans and for most of Easter Island's moai.

saladin.name: Saladin
saladin.summary: Founder of the Ayyubid dynasty and first sultan of Egypt and Syria (c. 1137 to 1193), who led the Muslim military effort against the Crusader states during the Third Crusade.

zara-yaqob.name: Zara Yaqob
zara-yaqob.summary: Emperor of Ethiopia from 1434 to 1468 who ruled under the throne name Constantine I; one historian called him the greatest Ethiopian ruler since the ancient Aksumite king Ezana.

fakhr-al-din-mosque.name: Fakhr al-Din Mosque
fakhr-al-din-mosque.summary: A mosque dating to 1269 in Mogadishu's Hamar Weyne district, built of marble and coral stone and named after the first sultan of the Mogadishu Sultanate.

sultanate-of-mogadishu.name: Sultanate of Mogadishu
sultanate-of-mogadishu.summary: Medieval Muslim sultanate centred in southern Somalia that became a major regional power with its own currency and a vast trading network dominating the gold trade.

david-roden-buxton.name: David Roden Buxton
david-roden-buxton.summary: British entomologist and British Council employee (1910 to 2003), best known for books on Russian architecture, ancient Ethiopian churches and the wooden churches of Eastern Europe.

great-mosque-of-kilwa.name: Great Mosque of Kilwa
great-mosque-of-kilwa.summary: Partly ruined former Friday mosque on Kilwa Kisiwani island in Tanzania, likely founded in the tenth century. Ibn Battuta described its great dome after visiting in 1331, and it was abandoned in the 18th century.

sahn.name: Sahn
sahn.summary: Courtyard in Islamic architecture, especially the formal courtyard of a mosque. Most traditional mosques have a large central one, surrounded on all sides by an arcade called a riwaq.

jesus.name: Jesus
jesus.summary: A 1st-century Jewish preacher in Roman Judaea regarded by Christians as the Messiah and central figure of Christianity, whose life is recorded chiefly in the Gospels.

adadi-mariam.name: Adadi Mariam
adadi-mariam.summary: Rock-hewn monolithic church roughly 66 km southwest of Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, a popular tourist site believed built in the 12th century.

merca.name: Merca
merca.summary: A historic port city in Somalia's Lower Shebelle province, about 109 km southwest of Mogadishu; traditional home of the Bimal clan and center of the Bimal revolt.

mombasa.name: Mombasa
mombasa.summary: Kenya's oldest city, founded around 900 CE, and once the first capital of British East Africa before Nairobi; long a major Indian Ocean trading port.

malindi.name: Malindi
malindi.summary: Town on Kenya's Indian Ocean coast, historically known as Melinde, located near Mombasa.

al-hasan-ibn-sulaiman.name: Al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman
al-hasan-ibn-sulaiman.summary: Sultan of Kilwa, in present-day Tanzania, from 1310 to 1333, nicknamed "father of gifts". He was one of Kilwa's most prosperous rulers before Portuguese contact, known for his generosity and his military, economic and building programs.

arba-a-rukun-mosque.name: Arba'a Rukun Mosque
arba-a-rukun-mosque.summary: A mosque in the Shangani medieval district of Mogadishu, Somalia.

mihrab.name: Mihrab
mihrab.summary: A niche in a mosque's wall marking the qibla, the direction of Mecca, toward which Muslims face when praying.

yekuno-amlak.name: Yekuno Amlak
yekuno-amlak.summary: First Emperor of the Ethiopian Empire (1270-1285) and founder of the Solomonic dynasty, which lasted until 1974, after defeating the last Zagwe king.

solomonic-dynasty.name: Solomonic dynasty
solomonic-dynasty.summary: Ruling dynasty of the Ethiopian Empire from the 13th to 20th centuries, founded in 1270 by Yekuno Amlak and claiming descent from the biblical Solomon; ended in 1974 with Haile Selassie's overthrow.

solomon.name: Solomon
solomon.summary: King of the united Kingdom of Israel, traditionally dated to about 970–931 BCE, famed in the Bible for his wealth, wisdom and the temple built in his name.

queen-of-sheba.name: Queen of Sheba (Makeda)
queen-of-sheba.summary: A figure first mentioned in the Hebrew Bible who brought gifts to King Solomon; her story was later elaborated in Jewish, Ethiopian Christian and Islamic tradition, though her existence is disputed.

amda-seyon-i.name: Amda Seyon I
amda-seyon-i.summary: Emperor of Ethiopia from 1314 to 1344, remembered in a later chronicle as a heroic warrior against neighboring Muslim states.

dawit-i.name: Dawit I
dawit-i.summary: Emperor of Ethiopia from 1382 to 1413 whose 33-year reign, following earlier conquests, is seen as a period of consolidation for the Solomonic kingdom.

ifat-historical-region.name: Ifat
ifat-historical-region.summary: A historical Muslim region in the Horn of Africa, located on the eastern edge of Shewa.

shotel.name: Shotel
shotel.summary: A curved sword from Tigray in northern Ethiopia and southern-central Eritrea, with an almost semicircular double-edged blade about a meter long and a rhinoceros-horn hilt.

yetbarak.name: Yetbarak
yetbarak.summary: A king of Ethiopia's Zagwe dynasty, said by historian Taddesse Tamrat to have been the son of Lalibela.

gafat-people.name: Gafat
gafat-people.summary: Extinct ethnic group once living along Ethiopia's Blue Nile, later pushed south of Gojjam and eventually treated as outcasts by the Amhara.

sultanate-of-shewa.name: Sultanate of Shewa
sultanate-of-shewa.summary: Muslim kingdom in present-day Ethiopia founded by the Arab Makhzumi dynasty, whose rise coincided with the decline of the Kingdom of Axum.

yeshaq-i.name: Yeshaq I
yeshaq-i.summary: Emperor of Ethiopia from 1414 to 1429/1430, a member of the Solomonic dynasty and second son of Emperor Dawit I.

greek-fire.name: Greek fire
greek-fire.summary: An incendiary weapon used by the Byzantine Empire from the 7th to 14th centuries, likely based on petroleum, that could burn on water and made it a fearsome naval weapon.

sultanate-of-ifat.name: Sultanate of Ifat
sultanate-of-ifat.summary: Medieval Muslim state in the Horn of Africa, also called Wafāt or the Kingdom of Zeila, ruled by the Walashma dynasty between the late 13th and early 15th centuries.

mora-historical-region.name: Mora
mora-historical-region.summary: A historical Muslim state in the Horn of Africa, positioned north of Ifat near Aussa in modern Ethiopia, neighboring states such as Adal and Hadiya.

walashma-dynasty.name: Walashma dynasty
walashma-dynasty.summary: A medieval Muslim dynasty founded in the 13th century in Ifat, ruling territory in the Horn of Africa now part of Somalia, Djibouti, Eritrea and eastern Ethiopia.

harar.name: Harar
harar.summary: Walled city in eastern Ethiopia, a long-standing trading hub linking the Horn of Africa to Arabia and beyond, called by UNESCO the 'fourth holiest city' of Islam.

jamal-ad-din-i.name: Jamal ad-Din I
jamal-ad-din-i.summary: A mid-14th-century governor of Ifat, son of Nahwi b. Mansur b. Umar Walashma and brother of Haqq ad-Din I.

haqq-ad-din-ii.name: Haqq ad-Din II
haqq-ad-din-ii.summary: Sultan of the Ifat Sultanate in the late 14th century who moved its capital to the Harar plateau, earning him credit as founder of the Adal Sultanate.

sa-ad-ad-din-ii.name: Sa'ad ad-Din II
sa-ad-ad-din-ii.summary: Sultan of the Ifat Sultanate who reigned from around 1386 to 1403 or 1410, remembered as the last great ruler of Ifat.

battle-of-gomit.name: Battle of Gomit
battle-of-gomit.summary: A 1445 battle in which the Ethiopian Empire under Emperor Zara Yaqob defeated the Adal Sultanate's army, killing Sultan Badlay ibn Sa'ad ad-Din.

chewa-regiments.name: Chewa regiments
chewa-regiments.summary: The feudal warrior class of Imperial Ethiopia, given land grants for military service whose settlements helped found many towns in Ethiopia and Eritrea.

ge-ez.name: Ge'ez
ge-ez.summary: Ancient South Semitic language from Ethiopia and Eritrea, still used today as the liturgical language of Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox and Catholic churches.

amharic.name: Amharic
amharic.summary: An Ethio-Semitic language and Ethiopia's official working language, spoken by over 58 million people; it is the second most widely spoken Semitic language after Arabic.

tigrinya-language.name: Tigrinya language
tigrinya-language.summary: An Ethio-Semitic language spoken by Tigrinya and Tigrayan peoples in Eritrea and Ethiopia, which developed separately from Ge'ez.

tigre-language.name: Tigre language
tigre-language.summary: An Ethio-Semitic language spoken mainly by the Tigre people of western Eritrea, closely related to Ge'ez, with about 800,000 speakers as of 1997.

kebra-nagast.name: Kebra Nagast
kebra-nagast.summary: A 14th-century Ethiopian national epic claiming the Solomonic dynasty descended from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba through their son Menelik I, giving religious legitimacy to Ethiopia's rulers.

menelik-i.name: Menelik I
menelik-i.summary: In Ethiopian legend, the reputed first Emperor of the Solomonic dynasty, said to be the son of King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba according to the 14th-century Kebra Nagast.

richard-pankhurst-historian.name: Richard Pankhurst
richard-pankhurst-historian.summary: British scholar (1927–2017), a founding member of the Institute of Ethiopian Studies and professor at the University of Addis Ababa, known for research on Ethiopian economic and socio-cultural history.

fetha-negest.name: Fetha Negest
fetha-negest.summary: A theocratic legal code compiled around 1240 by a Coptic Egyptian writer, later translated into Ge'ez in Ethiopia and used as its supreme law until 1931.

alexander-the-great.name: Alexander the Great
alexander-the-great.summary: King of Macedon from 336 BC who conquered much of the known world by age 30, creating an empire stretching from Greece to India; tutored by Aristotle.

old-dongola.name: Old Dongola
old-dongola.summary: A now-deserted Nubian town on the Nile in Sudan, capital of the medieval kingdom of Makuria from the 4th to 14th century, later replaced by modern Dongola downstream.

enrico-cerulli.name: Enrico Cerulli
enrico-cerulli.summary: Italian scholar of Somali and Ethiopian studies, as well as a governor and diplomat during and after Italian Fascism, who lived from 1898 to 1988.

yem-people.name: Yem people
yem-people.summary: An ethnic group in southwestern Ethiopia who speak Yemsa, an Omotic language, neighboring the Gurage, Hadya, Kembata and Jimma Oromo peoples.

newaya-krestos.name: Newaya Krestos (Sayf Ar'ed)
newaya-krestos.summary: Emperor of Ethiopia from 1344 to 1372, whose throne name, meaning "sword of terror," and wars with neighboring Muslims likely inspired the villain of a 15th-century Arabic epic.

hydraulic-empire.name: Hydraulic empire
hydraulic-empire.summary: A government structure that maintains power by controlling water resources for irrigation and flood control, requiring centralized bureaucracy.

shebelle-river.name: Shebelle River
shebelle-river.summary: A roughly 1,820-kilometre river rising in Ethiopia's highlands and flowing through Somalia toward Mogadishu, historically known as the Nile of Mogadishu.

jubba-river.name: Jubba River
jubba-river.summary: A river in southern Somalia flowing from the Ethiopian border south to the Somali Sea, giving its name to the surrounding Jubaland region.

amba-geshen.name: Mountain of the Princes
amba-geshen.summary: A mountain in northern Ethiopia (Amba Geshen) where male heirs to the Emperor were confined, often for life, to prevent them from challenging the throne.

rock-hewn-churches-lalibela.name: Rock-Hewn Churches of Lalibela
rock-hewn-churches-lalibela.summary: Eleven monolithic churches carved from rock in Ethiopia's highlands, commissioned by King Lalibela of the Zagwe dynasty to recreate Jerusalem; still used for worship and pilgrimage.

haqq-ad-din-i.name: Haqq ad-Din I
haqq-ad-din-i.summary: Sultan of the Ifat Sultanate (flourished 1328) who turned earlier sporadic raids into a full-scale religious war against Christian Abyssinia; some historians describe him as an ethnic Somali ruler.

wedem-arad.name: Wedem Arad
wedem-arad.summary: Emperor of Ethiopia from 1299 to 1314 and member of the Solomonic dynasty, who seized power from his nephews and died in 1314.

council-of-constance.name: Council of Constance
council-of-constance.summary: An ecumenical council of the Catholic Church held from 1414 to 1418 that ended the Western Schism by electing Pope Martin V and condemned the reformer Jan Hus as a heretic.

taddesse-tamrat.name: Taddesse Tamrat
taddesse-tamrat.summary: An Ethiopian historian (1935–2013) best known for his 1972 book Church and State in Ethiopia, 1270–1520, a foundational work in Ethiopian studies.

agaw-people.name: Agaw
agaw-people.summary: A Cushitic ethnic group of Ethiopia's northern highlands and Eritrea, speaking the Agaw (Central Cushitic) languages; many historically practiced a 'Hebraic religion' and included Beta Israel Jews.

sabr-ad-din-iii.name: Sabr ad-Din III
sabr-ad-din-iii.summary: Somali Sultan of the Adal Sultanate and son of Sa'ad ad-Din II, who defeated the Ethiopians and founded the Adal dynasty; died in 1422 or 1423.

fatagar.name: Fatagar
fatagar.summary: A historical province in the medieval Horn of Africa that separated Muslim and Christian territories, later becoming a central district and birthplace of Ethiopian emperors in the 15th century.

eleni-of-ethiopia.name: Eleni of Ethiopia
eleni-of-ethiopia.summary: Empress of Ethiopia by marriage to Zara Yaqob, who acted as regent from 1507 to 1516 and adviser to several emperors, until her death in 1522.

eskender.name: Eskender
eskender.summary: Emperor of Ethiopia (1471–1494) of the Solomonic dynasty who fought the Adal Sultanate and hosted the Portuguese envoy Pedro de Covilham at his court.

shewa.name: Shewa
shewa.summary: A historical region of Ethiopia, once an autonomous kingdom within the Ethiopian Empire, whose territory includes the modern capital Addis Ababa.

awash-river.name: Awash River
awash-river.summary: A major river of Ethiopia and the principal stream of a large drainage basin now considered the country's most developed and populous.

patristics.name: Patristics
patristics.summary: The study of early Christian writers known as Church Fathers, covering the Patristic era from about 100 CE to the mid-5th or late-8th century.

argobba-people.name: Argobba
argobba-people.summary: A Muslim ethnic group in northern and eastern Ethiopia known historically as skilled traders, now considered endangered due to exogamy and destitution.

gondarine-period.name: Gondarine period
gondarine-period.summary: Period of Ethiopian history from Emperor Fasilides's rise in 1632 to the decentralized 'Era of the Princes' in 1769, marked by Gondar's founding and achievements in art and architecture.

harla-people.name: Harla people
harla-people.summary: Ethnic group that once inhabited parts of Ethiopia, Somalia and Djibouti, speaking the Harla language of the Afroasiatic family.

chelenqo.name: Chelenqo
chelenqo.summary: A town in eastern Ethiopia near Harar, historically located in the Chercher region.

munesa.name: Munesa
munesa.summary: A district (woreda) in Ethiopia's Oromia Region, in the Arsi Zone near the Great Rift Valley, with its administrative center at Kersa.

lake-langano.name: Lake Langano
lake-langano.summary: A lake in Ethiopia's Oromia Region, in the Main Ethiopian Rift south of the capital, Addis Ababa.
